en: Preface to the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* Miracles (*Jūyì*) by Zhang Qiqiu, Palace Attendant Wang Shao,
Sun Xian, Monk Zhideng, and Wang Conggui’s Sister.
Chen Zhao of Wubuo, Left Camp; Sengweigong;
Dong Jinchao; Wang Qian; Seng Huizong; Seng Fazheng;
Śrāmaṇera Daoyin; and Wang Zhongan.
He Qin’s wife Wang Yin; Zhao An;
Wang Han; Gao She; the watchtower guard of Fengzhou, Wang Xiaolian.
Preface to the *Jiuyi* (Strange Tales) of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*,
compiled by Duan Chengshi, known as Ke Gu, Junior Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices during the Tang Dynasty.
In the seventeenth year of the Zhenyuan era, my late father traveled from Jing (one source reads Qi) to Shu to respond to the summons of Wei Nankang (Prince Wei Gao).

Toward the end of Wei’s life, he was slandered by the rebel Pei, who consequently appointed him Acting Magistrate of Lingchi County. Shortly thereafter, Wei passed away, and the rebel Pei assumed authority as the Acting Regent.
My late father had long been at odds with Pei; upon hearing this, he departed the county that very night and arrived at—
At the eastern gate of the city, a notice was posted shortly after it was opened, forbidding officials from various districts from leaving their respective counties.

That evening, amidst a dark wind, as he returned and had traveled two *li* beyond the city wall, he saw two torches flanking the road, leading the way for a hundred paces. At first, he thought it was district officials coming to welcome him.

Furthermore, I found it strange that he did not proceed further; yet his estimation of heights, depths, distances, and nearness was unerring. Only when we were about to reach the county walls did the fire vanish.

When I questioned the county officials, they had not yet received the official notice from the prefecture. At that time, my late father had been reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for five or six years, without a single day of omission.

This proves that utmost sincerity must surely evoke a response, and that where there is a response, there is inevitably a manifestation. The guiding flame of the past was, in fact, produced by the power of the sutra.
This is the outward manifestation. Later, as his rebellious conduct gradually became apparent, an imperial edict appointed Yuan Gongzi as the Regional Commander (Jiedushi).

Chengshi’s second cousin, who had served in the military from his youth, was in charge of the Left Guard. Fearing he would be implicated in the disaster, he conspired with the Military Inspector to communicate with Yuan using wax-sealed pellets and silk letters.
The plot was soon discovered, and they were all slaughtered like fish and meat. The rebels claimed that my late father had known of their scheme.
At that time, his late father was reciting a sutra; after a long night had passed, he did not realize it. Because he had fallen asleep, the doors were all closed.

Suddenly waking up, he heard someone open the door and enter, saying "Do not be afraid" two or three times. Then, as if an object had struck the altar, there was a sudden, explosive sound. As he started up in alarm, the voice was still ringing in his ears.

He looked around at those on his left and right; his attendants and servants were all fast asleep. He ordered a candle made of birch bark to be lit and searched everywhere, but found nothing at first.

What I saw was that the door bolt which had been there before was already opened. My late father had maintained this sutra more than one hundred thousand times, and the signs of its efficacy were most manifest.
Chengshi recently observed that from the Jin and Song dynasties onward, people of the time have all composed biographies to clarify these matters.
Furthermore, following his instructions, I have received and maintained it, and since the Tang dynasty, the *Record of Miraculous Responses of the Diamond Sutra* has appeared.
Three fascicles. Chengshi (Duan Chengshi) received the imperial command to uphold and expound [this work].

In the second year of the Taihe era, he listened to a single recitation of the *Píngxiāo* Imperial Commentary from the monk Xījiǎn at Yangzhou. In the sixth year, he listened to a single recitation of the *Dànyún* Commentary from the monk Jìngshē at Jingzhou.
In the first year of the Kāichéng era, he listened to the *Qīnglóng* [Commentary] from Master Huáichǔ in the Capital.

Having recited the commentary once, I shall continue to recite and transcribe it daily, hoping that its illumination may reach those who have no limit and that it may circulate throughout my entire life.
I shall collect lost and omitted passages to supplement deficiencies in Buddhist rites, titling this work *The Extraordinary Anecdotes of the Diamond Sūtra*.

Regarding Zhang Qiqiu, the late Minister Zhang Yi’s father, Qiqiu was a fervent believer in the teachings of Śākyamuni. Every morning, he would change his robes and, holding a scripture, recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* fifteen times before the image [of the Buddha].
He practiced this for several decades without slackening. At the beginning of the Yongtai era, he served as the Chancellor of Shuo...

At that time, there was a minor general within the headquarters of the Regional Commander who, burdened by guilt and fearing his crimes would be exposed, incited several hundred soldiers to plot a rebellion.
While Qi Qiu was strolling idly in the small hall after the official court session had ended, suddenly dozens of soldiers appeared.

With his blade bared, he fled inside. Qiū’s attendants were all merely slaves; they rushed toward the main gate, but after traveling only a few paces past the small hall, they looked back and saw no one.
Suspecting it was a ghostly apparition, they reached the gate, where their wives, daughters, and servants called out from within, saying:
"There are two armored warriors whose bodies emerge from atop the hall. At that moment, the military guards of the yamen heard the commotion and took up their positions.
The soldiers entered in a state of turmoil and arrived before the small hall. There they saw more than ten men standing rigidly in the courtyard with their hands hanging down and mouths agape.
The soldiers cast their weapons to the ground, and the group subsequently captured and bound them. Five or six of them were mute and unable to speak; the others confessed, saying:

"As we were about to ascend the hall, we suddenly saw two armored warriors several *zhang* tall who glared at us and shouted. At first, it was as if we had been struck by a sudden affliction. Qiū [Zhì] was present.
Upon hearing this, he consequently renounced wine and meat. Zhang Fengxiang was an official in my gate; Lu Mai was his maternal cousin’s husband, who said to me:
"The虞候 (yuhou) Wang..."
While Liu Yihuai was in Bianzhou, Han Hong served as the Right Chamberlain, and a certain Wang served as the Left Chamberlain. Wang and Hong were close friends.

Some said that the two men were manipulating military affairs and intended to act against Liu’s interests. Liu became greatly incensed and summoned both of them for interrogation. Han Hong was Liu’s nephew;
he pressed his head against the ground, smashed his own head, and spoke with great vehemence. Consequently, Liu’s anger subsided slightly. Wang—
In my old age, my thighs trembled and I could not defend myself. Liu Chiling pulled me down and sentenced me to thirty strokes of the staff. At that time, new red clubs had been made;
their heads were several inches in diameter and were bound with sinew and lacquer. Had I not been spared by chance, I would have died after only five or six blows.
Han thought that he must surely be dead. When dusk fell, he went to his house and was surprised to find no sound of weeping; he further surmised that [Wang] was afraid and dared not cry.
Upon inquiring of the gatekeeper, he was told, "The Great Envoy is unharmed. As Hong-su was well-acquainted with him, he proceeded to the inner chamber and questioned him.
Wang said, "I have been reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for forty years, and only now am I beginning to gain its power," as he spoke while still seated.
At that time, he saw a giant hand, as large as a winnowing basket, suddenly covering his back. He then bared his shoulder to show it to Han, but there were no marks from the lash at all.

Han had previously disliked the followers of Śākyamuni, but because of this incident, he began to associate with the monks. Every day he would personally transcribe ten sheets of paper, until the accumulated total reached several hundred fascicles.
Later, while serving in the Secretariat, during the height of summer, an official of remonstrance came to visit him on business; at that moment, Han was bathing.
When [the Emperor] saw the transcribed sutras, he questioned him with astonishment. Han then related in detail the matter concerning Wang Shao. "I hold the office of Attendant-in-Ordinary at Jixian;
Lord Liu told me of this."
Sun Xian Liang Chongyi was in Xiangzhou. Before the outbreak of hostilities, a minor general named Sun Xian died suddenly.
After two nights, he revived and dreamed that he arrived at a place like the residence of a sovereign, where the ceremonial guards were extremely strict. An official led him to meet a monk.

Regarding the case of the monk whose dharma name was Huixiu: he had been deceased for a year. During his lifetime, he had gravely violated the precepts, and upon entering the underworld, there were no good deeds to be recorded of him.
He then falsely claimed, "I always instructed my grandson Xian to copy the Lotus Sutra; therefore, Xian has been summoned to face questioning."
Because Xian had never before questioned the monks, he held onto his position for some time without reaching a decision. Suddenly, he saw a śramaṇa who said, "The Venerable Kṣitigarbha has told me:
'If you, disciple, confess your fault, you will also receive protection. Xian then followed these words and consequently escaped harm.
Furthermore, it is said that during the interrogation, he saw a King of the Rong (戎) dynasty accompanied by several hundred guards approaching from outside.

The Lord of Hell descended the steps, and they ascended the hall together to take their seats. Not long after, a great wind swept them away. He also saw a man undergoing torture for the examination of his sins and merits;
this man had constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* but also enjoyed eating meat. On his left were several thousand scrolls of the sutra, while on his right...
The flesh piled up at the edges formed a mountain. Because the meat was so vast, it was about to be brought under the weight of a grave discourse.
Suddenly, a single spark of fire flew from within the heap toward the mountain of flesh; in an instant, it was completely consumed. The man then departed, walking through the air.
Everyone asked Dizang, "Where has the wind that blew the foreign king just now gone? Dizang replied, "That king shall enter the Avīci Hell; as for the wind that blew just now—"
This was the wind of karma. Because he had led them all to look into hell, the smoke and flames at the gate flared fiercely, and the sound was like wind and thunder;
they were so terrified that they did not dare to look. As they approached the cauldron of boiling water, a splash of foam fell upon his left thigh, and the pain pierced to his very marrow.

Dizang then ordered an official to escort him back, forbidding him from leaking any matters of the underworld. Upon returning, it was as if he had been in a dream, while his wife and children wept around him.

One day having passed, he consequently disbanded his household to copy scriptures and requested ordination. At the spot where [the blood] had dripped in his dream, an ulcer formed that did not heal throughout his life.
This was the monk Zhideng.

During the Zhenyuan era, the monk Zhideng of Tianchong Temple in Jingzhou constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When he fell ill and died, his disciples found that his hands and feet remained warm;
they did not place him in a coffin for seven days, after which he returned to life. He said: "At first, I saw someone in the underworld who appeared to be a king.
Because I had been reciting the sutra, he joined his palms and descended from the steps. He then greeted me, saying, 'I grant the Master ten more years.'"

Nianzai Shi said, "One must strive throughout one's life to transcend birth and death. He further asked, "Among the monastics of the human realm, there are those who eat *yiyiren* (coix lacryma) and medicinal foods after midday;

this greatly contravenes the fundamental teachings. Deng replied, "Regarding the provisions in the Vinaya concerning what is permitted (*kai*) and what is prohibited (*zhe*), how should one understand them?
[Nianzai] said, "These were added by later generations and do not reflect the Buddha’s intention. Now, among the monastic community of Jingzhou, there are none who consume medicine after midday.
The King followed his noble younger sister to the people of Gongan and Chanling Forest. Before the noble younger sister had married, she constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

During the Zhengyuan era, she suddenly died of a violent illness. Three days after she had been buried, her family [the *Guangji* edition reads "covered" the tomb] heard groaning from within the grave.
He then opened [the coffin] to look inside; indeed, there was a breath of life, and he was brought back home. After several days, he was able to speak. He said:
"When I first arrived in the underworld, the officials there released me to return because of my merit in upholding the scriptures.
King Conggui was skilled at carpentry and frequently constructed buildings at Linghua Temple in Gong’an. This the Dharma Master Shu heard from Conggui many times.

During the time when Wu Bo of the Left Wing was stationed in Sichuan under the command of Wei Nan’gang, there was a soldier of the Left Wing who, while at the western mountain training camp, studied the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with his fellow fire-guard comrades.
Being by nature stubborn, it took him a full day on the first day to master the titles of the chapters. That night, he went outside the fort to gather firewood.

He was bound by the barbarian cavalry and taken away. After traveling over a hundred *li*, they stopped. Before dawn had broken, they threw him to the ground, tied his hair to a wooden stake, covered him with camel wool, and lay upon him.
This man thought only of the title of a sutra; suddenly he saw a piece of gold the size of a ladle emitting light that came to rest before him.
He tried to lift his head and move his body, and all his bonds fell away. He then rose stealthily and pursued the gold.
He fled on foot. He calculated that he had traveled no more than ten or so li before dawn, yet he was unaware that he had already arrived home.
His home was in the eastern market of the prefecture. When his wife and children first saw him, they suspected he was a ghost; he then related the circumstances of his arrival in detail.

Five or six days after his arrival, the commander of the military camp finally reported his escape. At first Wei did not believe it, but since the date of his escape and the date of his arrival home matched exactly, he was finally spared.
At the beginning of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Zhaozong’s reign, Chen Zhao, a clerk in the administrative office (*kongmu*) of Hanzhou, fell ill.
He saw a man dressed in yellow clothing approach his bedside and say, "Judge Zhao summons you. Zhao asked for the reason; the man replied that he had come from the underworld, where Liu Pi was...
Dong Xuan was facing interrogation and required Zhao to serve as his witness. Zhao remained seated for a while when another man appeared, holding an object like a ball.
The official before him marveled at the delay, and the man replied, "I was waiting for the butcher's shop to open.
He then laughed and said to Zhao, "Do not be afraid. To take the breath of a living person, one must obtain a pig’s bladder; you may stand to the side facing east."

Zhao lay down as he had been told. Unaware of the time that had passed, he found himself following two officials along a very level road for some ten li or so, until they reached a city as large as a provincial capital, where armored soldiers guarded the gates. Upon entering, he saw a man with a terrifyingly wrathful countenance;
this was Officer Zhao. Zhao said, "Liu Pi has seized Dongchuan. Dou Xuan has captured forty-seven head of cattle."

When sent to Zizhou, he was judged according to the decree that Pí was to be executed. It was further stated: "Previously, you served as the clerk for the *kǒngmù* (administrative records), so you ought to know the facts of the matter.
Before he could respond, he heard from across the wall the voice of Dòu calling out, asking after Chén Zhāo’s well-being and inquiring about the survival of his brothers, wife, and children.
Zhāo immediately wished to go and meet him, but the official of the underworld said: "The appearance of Lord Dòu is extremely hideous; [you must not see him]."
He wished to see him. Zhao then fully explained the truth regarding the killing of the ox, stating that it was in accordance with the detailed instructions of Official Liu, not a formal document.
The paper was made of hemp; its surface was currently stored on a shelf in a certain office in Hanzhou. He immediately ordered an official to take it there.

When Zhao arrived in Hanzhou to retrieve it, the gates and halls were locked. He then entered and exited through a small keyhole. After he had delivered the instructions until they were fully implemented, Zhao remained silent. Zhao.
"Zhao, do you know that you yourself have committed one transgression? When Dou Xuan slaughtered the ox, you took one of the heads for yourself.
Before Zhao could respond, he said, "This is not like the human world; falsehoods cannot be excused. In a moment, a soldier appeared carrying the ox head.

Zhao was immediately struck with terror and begged for mercy. Zhao ordered that the legal codes be consulted, and it was determined that he should receive one hundred strokes of the rod and five years of penal servitude.
On the tenth day, Zhao asked Zhaozao, "What merits do you possess? Zhao immediately recounted her deeds: she had provided vegetarian feasts for several people and painted certain Buddhist images.
Zhao said, "These are the conditions for your future life. Zhaozao spoke again, saying that she had once recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at her cousin’s house.
Zhao said, "You should join your palms and request it. Zhaozao did as instructed. After a short while, she saw a yellow-bound scripture descend from the sky.
Zhaowu then went down and stayed before the official. Zhao took it and looked at it; it was the very copy his elder cousin had borrowed, and the burnt spots were still visible.
Zhao then ordered him to join his palms, and the scripture immediately vanished. Zhao said, "This will suffice to avoid [punishment].

He then released him and sent him back to another office, saying, "The lifespan allotted by birth shall be examined for its length or brevity. A clerk reported, "Zhaowu’s original name was Jiao; this is the 'jiao' with the 'gold' radical."
When the year arrived for Dao (the sword) to be changed to Zhao, eighteen years had passed.
Zhao heard this and felt despondent. Zhao Xiao said, "In these eighteen years, you have enjoyed great pleasures; why are you not pleased? He then ordered an official to escort Zhao on his way.
Midway, they encountered a horse blocking the road. The official said, "This is your original possession that you may ride. If you mount it now, you shall live; otherwise, you are already dead."
It was already midday.
The monk Weigong,
a monk from Faxon Temple in Jingzhou, had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* fifty times every day for over thirty years.

He disregarded monastic decorum and was fond of wine, which led to much strife; consequently, he was detested by the assembly of monks. Later, when he fell ill and was about to die, there was a monk named Lingkui in the same monastery whose conduct was similar to that of Weigong.
These two were a bane to the temple. On one occasion, Lingkui went out on some business;

after traveling one *li* from the monastery, he encountered five or six young men who were exceptionally handsome and dressed in fresh, clean garments. Each of them held a musical instrument. As they...
The Kucha school asked Lingkui, "Where is the venerable Weigong? Lingkui immediately told them his location.
Suspecting that there might be offerings at his temple, they returned to the monastery in the evening. Upon hearing the sound of the bells, they found that Weigong had already passed away.
He then recounted what he had seen earlier; on that day, the entire monastery heard the sound of stringed and wind instruments, yet no musicians entered the temple. At that time, he was renowned...
The monk said, "Weigong was able to be reborn in the Land of Immovability precisely because of the power of the sutras; he used this account to encourage Lingkui.
Lingkui was moved to realization and humbled himself before the monastic community.
Dong Jinzhao, Dong Jinzhao.
During the Yuanhe era, he entered the military. When he was first stationed in the army, he was on night duty atop the tower to the east of the city.
One night, under the bright moon, he suddenly saw four men dressed in yellow approaching from the east and gathering beneath the city wall. They spoke their own names and appearances.
As they were being pursued, they spoke among themselves, saying: "Dong Jinchao regularly recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
With one portion of its merit, he prays for the protection of the underworld authorities. We have long benefited from his kindness; how could we kill him?
We must sacrifice our lives to take his place. If this man departs, we shall have no one to rely upon. One of them said: "Opposite Dong Jinchao's door is..."
"There is one person of the same surname, the same age, and a similar life span who can serve as his substitute. Having said this, he suddenly vanished.

When [the official] entered the court the next day, everyone was struck with wonder. At dawn, they heard the voice of a soul returning from across the door. When asked about the reason, the parents of the deceased said: [as follows].
The son died suddenly last night. When Jinchao learned of it, he wept with emotion; Sui-zhi then performed the funeral rites for him and provided for his parents.
Later, the boy left the household life, taking the Dharma name Huitong and residing at Tang’an Temple in Xingyuan.

(Initially, Lu Qizhi harbored doubts about this, but later those who understood the matter remarked that since their lifespans were comparable, it was not a case of an untimely death; thus his doubts were resolved.)
During the Yuanhe era, while Minister of Works Yan Shou was in Jiangling, Wang Mian, the Commandant of the Cenyang Garrison, regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra*.
Once, while returning from a mission to investigate affairs in Guizhou, his boat was wrecked at Zhata滩 (Zhata Rapids), and five people were drowned together. At first, Wang Mian...
He entered the water. Someone handed him a bamboo pole, which he held as it rose and fell with the waves. Upon reaching Xiàláo Town, he reached the shore and did not die.
Looking at the object in his hand, he saw it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that had been given to him. From Zhàtān to Xiàláo is over three hundred li.
Senghui of Gong’an, Jingzhou:
Senghui of Gong’an, Jingzhou, whose secular surname was Cai, frequently suffered from the effects of sorcery until he became so emaciated that his bones showed through his skin.

He then made a vow to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* while awaiting his end; by the time he had reached fifty recitations, he dreamed one day during the day that someone commanded him to open his mouth.
He drew out more than ten strands of hair from his throat. At night, he again dreamed that he spat out a large earthworm one cubit long.
From this, his illness was subsequently cured. The monk Xingjian of Mount Jing witnessed these events.
The monk Fǎzhèng was a resident of the Kāiyuán Monastery in Jiānglíng. A monk of the Prajñā Hall, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* thirty-seven times every day.

At the beginning of the Chángqìng era, he fell ill and passed away. Upon reaching the underworld, he encountered one who appeared like a king, who asked the Master what meritorious deeds he had performed throughout his life.

He replied, "Constantly recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Thereupon, [the King] invited him up to the palace and had him ascend the embroidered throne. He recited the sūtra seven times;
the attendants all joined their palms in reverence, and those below the steps who were being interrogated and cross-examined all ceased their activities to listen.

When the recitation was finished, he sent an official to escort him back. As the King descended the steps to see him off, he said, "Master, you shall remain among humans for another thirty years; do not let your practice decline."
While reciting the scriptures, he was traveling with an official for several tens of li when they reached a large pit.

The official then leaned over the edge of the pit and pushed him from behind, as if he had fallen into empty space. He had been dead for seven days; only his face was not cold. Fǎzhèng is still alive today at over eighty years of age.
The monk Chángjìng of Jingzhou personally witnessed this event.
The Śrāmaṇera Dàoyìn of Shíshǒu County:
There was a śrāmaṇera named Dàoyìn who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

At the beginning of the Bǎolì era (the *Guǎngjì* states it was the Chángqìng era), while returning home at night after having gone out on another errand, he suddenly encountered a tiger on the road that roared and lunged forward. Knowing he could not escape, the śrāmaṇera...
He sat with his eyes closed, silently reciting the sutra, vowing in his heart to provide protection. The tiger then crouched in the grass to guard him until dawn, when the villagers came and went;
the tiger then departed. When they looked at the spot where he had been crouching, they saw saliva flowing upon the ground.
In the third year of the Yuanhe era, the rebel Li Tongjie obstructed the military at Cangzhou. Emperor Jing ordered Liu You to lead the Qi-de Army to suppress him.
Initially, they besieged the city of Dezhou; though the city was strong, it could not be taken. The following day, they attacked it again, from the hour of Mao until the hour of Wei.
Nine out of ten were wounded, yet he could not finally pull it out. At that time, there was Wang Zhonggan, a soldier of the Eight Generals within the Yamen of Qizhou and a native of Boye.
He had constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for over twenty years, never missing a single day.
On that day, as Zhonggan ascended the flying ladder and his body was nearly at the top of the rampart, he was struck by arrows like a porcupine and knocked down by a rolling log. Together—
The fire suddenly dragged him out and placed him outside the city walls, on the bank within the moat. At that time, as the night fell, Chō ordered the withdrawal of the troops;
meanwhile, arrows rained down upon the city like rain. His comrades were in such a frantic rush that they forgot to retrieve the body of Chūkan.

Having died, Chūkan found himself as if in a dream in a desolate wilderness; encountering a great river, he wished to cross but had no means to do so. He looked up to heaven and wailed aloud. Suddenly—
Hearing the sound of human voices, Zhonggan saw a man over ten feet tall. Suspecting him to be a divine being, he asked for directions to the camp.
The man said, "Do not fear me; I shall enable you to cross this river. Zhonggan bowed to him.

Before his head had even risen from its prostration, the divine being seized him by the waist and hurled him into the air. Only after a long time did he land on the ground. Suddenly, as if awakening from a dream, he heard the sound of bandits.
It was the second watch on the city wall. At first he did not notice that he had waded through water, nor was he aware of his wound.

Raising his hand to touch his face, he saw blood smeared upon his eyebrows and eyelashes; only then did he realize he was injured. He then forced himself to walk forward, but after a hundred-odd paces, he collapsed.

Again, he saw the man from before holding a blade and shouting, "Up! Up, Zhonggan! Startled and terrified, he fled for more than a li before sitting down to rest, where he finally heard the original [sound].
The army raised a battle cry and reached their own camp. When he sought out his fellow soldiers, he learned that his body lay dead within the moat—the very river he had crossed in his dream.
Zhonggan was currently serving in the Qi-de Army.
He Qin’s wife, He Qin, made her living by trading goods. Her wife, Lady Liu, had abstained from alcohol and meat since her youth and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

She would first burn incense before the image [of the Buddha] and vow that her life would end at forty-five years of age and that her mind would remain undisturbed at the time of death. She knew the day of her own death beforehand. When the Tai... [year arrived].
In the winter of the fourth year of the Wuhé era, at the age of forty-five, he relinquished all his possessions and assets to provide for the monastic community.

Intending to enter the *sārvakālika* (year-round) retreat to bid farewell to his relatives and friends, Hé Zhěn claimed he was afflicted by a demonic possession and refused to believe [his resolve]. On the day of the New Year’s Eve, he invited monks to receive the precepts.

Upon entering the mountain pass, he bathed and changed his clothes, then stayed alone in a single room, sitting in the lotus posture and reciting the scriptures in a loud voice. When the light of dawn began to appear, it suddenly became silent. His children and grandchildren...
He opened the chamber to look inside; [the body] was already deceased. The crown of the head was so hot that it scorched the hand. Wáng Yīn buried him with the rites accorded to a monk.
The stupa is located at the northern outskirts of Jīngzhōu. Wáng Yīn.
Wang Yin, a soldier of the Left Regiment in Shu, regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and abstained from meat and alcohol. He served as a storekeeper for rewards and provisions;
on several occasions, he was mistakenly implicated by others and was repeatedly sentenced to death, yet each time he escaped by chance.

In the fourth year of the Taihe era, Guo Zhao, the Minister of Works (*Sikong*), was stationed in Shu. Guo was stern and impulsive; anyone who displeased him even slightly was put to death. Wang Yin...
He presented some cotton *mianxie* (dyed silk) as a gift, but Guo disliked its poor quality and ordered him to bare his back so that he might kill him.

Guo had a foreign dog that followed him wherever he lay or rose; it would bite anyone who was not a member of the household. Suddenly, after barking several times, the dog stood up and gripped Wang Yin’s back.
He drove [the dog] away, but it would not leave. Guo was astonished by this, and his anger was thereby dissipated.

Regarding the year when Zhao An left for Shu under the Protector Guo: there was a commoner named Zhao An who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. While traveling through the wilds...
Later, outside, he saw a bundle of clothes left by the side of a tomb. Because it had no owner, Dao’an took it back with him. Upon arriving home, he mentioned it to his wife and children.

A neighbor immediately reported this to the authorities, claiming that Dao’an had stolen property. He was arrested and sent to the county jail. The magistrate’s legal officer, enraged that he would not admit to the crime, seized his legs with a large gate-bar and snapped them into three pieces.
Later, the official ordered him to be flogged on the back; however, every time the staff struck him, it would break. The officer suspected there was something else about him.
Jianchu asked him about this, and he replied that he had been reciting only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When he reached Shenguo, Gao also marveled at him and released him.

Upon returning home, his wife said, "On such-and-such a day, I heard several loud cracks emanating from your scripture case; fearing something was wrong, I did not dare open it. Dao’an then rushed to look at it;
the binding cord was severed and the wooden rollers were broken, while the paper was completely torn apart. Dao’an is still alive today.
Wang Han of Taihe 5:
Wang Han, a commoner from Shifang County in Hanzhou, was habitually in the marketplace seeking small profits day after day.
Suddenly, he died a violent death. After three days had passed, he returned to life and said: "In the underworld, sixteen people were summoned together; fifteen..."

The people were dispersed to other locations, and Han went alone to one office. There he saw a youth in a green robe who claimed to be his nephew and served as a hall-attendant for the infernal officials.
He then led him to see the Director of Investigations, who further stated that the youth’s appearance was like his own elder brother’s; yet in both cases, they did not resemble each other at all.
His elder brother said to him, "There is an ox that has come to sue you, claiming that when you were clearing land by burning slash-and-burn, you unjustly burned it to death.
Furthermore, you once sold bamboo to a dog-killer to make a *konghou* lute; he killed two dogs, and the dogs have also come to sue you.

Your name is not yet registered in the death records, so you may still escape [retribution]. What meritorious deeds would you perform? Han wished to provide a vegetarian feast and transcribe [the scriptures] for them.

He said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* were both unsuitable. He then requested, "If you recite the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* seven times every day for me, I will give it to you.
His elder brother replied joyfully, "That is sufficient. Once he was restored to health, he abandoned his trade and left the household life; he is currently residing in Shifang County.
In the winter of the seventh year of the Taihe era, Li Gongshi, a Grand Master for Attending on the Emperor, served as the Military Commissioner (Xingjun Sima) of Taiyuan.
Gao She, the registrar (Kongmuguan), was staying overnight at the official residence when, at the hour the drums signaled the dawn watch, he went to a neighboring room and suddenly encountered a man.
He was over six chi tall. He called out, "The army commander is calling for you! Suo Jie then set off. As he walked somewhat slowly, the man pushed him from behind;
without realizing it, they headed north for about several tens of li. They reached a wild area and gradually entered the bottom of a valley.

Afterward, they climbed a mountain, and upon reaching the summit, they looked out in all directions; the villages and houses were all visible below them. A group of officials who had been pursuing him called out.
He said, "Follow me, Master She. Upon arriving at the center, many people were dressed in vermilion and green.

The person presiding over the case appeared to be Judge Cui Xingxin, who declared, "Hand this over to the officials for interrogation. They were then led out to another place where several hundred people sat in the open air, mingled with pigs and sheep.
They were brought before a man, who was none other than Du Ze, the brother-in-law of She. He addressed She, saying, "At first, you..."
When I received the letter, I established a new "Human Agency" (renxin ju) and sent someone to purchase four sheep; do you remember this?
Now I am being pursued by you and have endured bitter suffering. Suji said, "At that time, I merely ordered meat to be bought, not specifically sheep.
At this, he remained silent. Seeing a shepherd standing there and biting [the air], he hesitated, was led away, and in an instant, he saw another place.

In an open pavilion with square beams, large iron rings were nailed to the beams. Several hundred men, all holding knives and ropes, tied people’s heads and dragged them into the rings to gouge out their eyes and dismember them.
When Shi涉 (She) was terrified and fled, he did nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Suddenly, he encountered his old acquaintance Yang Yan, who said, "When Minister Li Shuo was in office, he executed the bandit Li Yingdao by beating him to death for robbery."
The matter of the bandit was concluded. For thirty years, he had been reborn in various places; now he returned to recount his previous affairs. "Do you still remember? he asked.
Zhao Sheng replied that because he was young at the time, he did not recall it. Furthermore, he encountered his old acquaintance Duan Yi, who had previously been his sworn brother.

Upon meeting Zhao Sheng, Duan asked, "Do you still recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without neglecting it? Zhao Sheng said, "What I have seen until now has not yet reached the ultimate."

"In this place of suffering, I have striven to cultivate wholesome karma, and that I am now able to return is due to the power of the sutras. Having said this, he was sent back home; it was as if in a dream.
Although he had already been dead for a night, the area where he had been dragged remained swollen and discolored for several days.
The Beacon Guard of Fengzhou during the early Yongtai era:
A beacon guard from Fengzhou went out at dusk and was captured by the Qiang. He entered Western Tibet to trade for horses;
the Tibetan commander ordered his shoulder bone to be perforated and passed through with a leather thong, assigning him several hundred head of horses. After half a year, the horses had multiplied.

The number increased tenfold. He was about to be rewarded with several hundred sheepskins; thus, he moved closer to the *yazhang* (tents) of the *btsan-po*. The *btsan-po*’s son, who appreciated his diligence, ordered him to hold the banner.
Whenever there were leftovers of meat or curd on the left and right, they were given to him. After another half-year had passed, he wept bitterly over the curd and meat and would not eat them.
When the *btsan-po* questioned him, he replied: "I have an elderly mother. Lately, she has frequently seen me in her dreams at night."
Pupo Ren heard this and was filled with regret. That night, he summoned him into his tent and said, "The laws of the barbarians are strict;
there is no precedent for allowing you to return. I shall give you two horses of great strength. Take them by such-and-such a path and flee home; say nothing of me.

The frontier watchman received the horses and galloped as fast as possible until both were exhausted and died. He then hid by day and fled by night. After several days, he was wounded in the foot by a thorn.

In the midst of the inverted sandbars, a wind suddenly blew, and something rustled past him. He reached out and grasped it to wrap around his feet; after a short while, the pain vanished. He tested walking and running, and he was as before.
After two nights and one day, he reached the borders of Fengzhou. Upon returning home, his mother was still alive. Overwhelmed by both grief and joy, he said:
"Ever since I lost you, I have done nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra*, never ceasing even for sleep or meals, praying for your recovery."
He saw this. Now, as the fruit of his vow, he took the sutra and prostrated before it; however, several fascicles had been torn and lost, and he did not know how this had come about.
Because [the son] spoke of the matter of injuring his foot on a desert crossing, his mother told him to remove his bandage and look at it.
What was wrapped around the wound were, in fact, several fascicles of the sutra; the wound also healed.

During the Dali era, a thief who had stolen a horse in Taiyuan falsely accused a man named Wang Xiaolian of complicity. After ten days of interrogation and torture, the victim was subjected to extreme suffering and was forced to confess.
The investigating official suspected the case was unjust and did not immediately finalize the indictment. The man thought only of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. His...
His voice was piteous and piercing, ceasing neither by day nor night. Suddenly one day, two bamboo joints fell into the prison and rolled right before him.
The other prisoners scrambled to seize them; the jailer, suspecting a blade might be hidden within, broke them open to look inside. There were two lines of writing that read:

"Even the Dharma should be relinquished, how much more so that which is not Dharma. The calligraphy was exceptionally fine. The leader of the bandits was filled with grief and remorse, and he fully confessed his crimes.
Concealing a grudge, he slandered him (*Guangji reads "old grudge").
*Jingang jing jiuyi* (End).
